paragraphs: A generalization bound connects a model's loss on training examples to its loss over the population it is meant to serve. This paper develops a family of such bounds using conditional mutual information, or CMI. Its distinguishing choice is to measure information through the losses produced by the learned hypothesis, rather than through the hypothesis itself.

The framework compares training and population losses with a jointly convex function and bounds that comparison using information evaluated sample by sample. Changing the comparison function lets the framework recover and extend earlier results. One particular choice, binary KL divergence, produces a samplewise average counterpart of Seeger's PAC-Bayesian bound.

In some scenarios, that new bound characterizes deep networks' population loss more tightly than previous bounds. The authors also derive high-probability versions of some average results and recover bounds for multiclass problems with finite Natarajan dimension. These results establish a common framework for several guarantees while keeping the reported improvement conditional on the scenario.
neurips-2022-a-new-family-of-generalizat.tldr: Measuring information through individual losses yields a unified family of generalization bounds, with tighter results in some deep-learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained with full-batch gradient descent often exhibit a distinctive pattern in loss sharpness. Sharpness here means the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, a measure of local curvature. It initially rises toward two divided by the step size, then fluctuates around that level in a regime called the edge of stability.

The paper studies how this behavior develops along training, organizing the trajectory into four phases according to changes in sharpness. Experiments identify the magnitude of the output-layer weights as a useful indicator of those changes. That observation guides theoretical and empirical efforts to explain how several quantities evolve and contribute to the behavior in each phase.

The authors also prove a sharpness result for two-layer fully connected linear networks under specified assumptions. This provides a theoretical account within a restricted model setting, alongside broader empirical observations. The contribution is an analysis of the dynamics behind the observed pattern, with the abstract explicitly acknowledging limits to the theory.
neurips-2022-analyzing-sharpness-along-g.tldr: The paper analyzes four phases of gradient-descent sharpness dynamics and proves edge-of-stability behavior for a restricted linear-network setting.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation regression uses knowledge from a relevant source domain to predict numerical outputs in a target domain. The paper proposes a neural network that makes the relationship between inputs and outputs aware of the domains' distributions. This distribution-informed construction becomes the basis of a general framework for transferring regression knowledge.

The framework encompasses approaches based on invariant representations, reweighting, and adaptive Gaussian processes. Bringing these approaches into one formulation helps explain their relationships and motivates efficient training with overparameterized networks. The authors also analyze convergence and provide a bound on generalization error, linking the proposed modeling approach to theoretical guarantees.

A distinctive part of the bound is how it measures the difference between domains. It uses maximum mean discrepancy in a function space induced by the network's neural tangent kernel, rather than a discrepancy in features chosen from hidden layers. Experiments across domain adaptation regression benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness. Together, the results connect distribution-aware prediction, existing adaptation methods, and a specific mathematical account of domain mismatch.
neurips-2022-distribution-informed-neura.tldr: Distribution-informed networks unify several regression adaptation approaches and support generalization analysis using a network-induced measure of domain mismatch.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression tries to recover a mathematical expression from observed function values. A common procedure first chooses the expression's structure and then fits its numerical constants through nonconvex optimization. Genetic programming repeats this process across evolving candidates, while earlier neural approaches predict an expression structure directly but remain less powerful.

This paper asks a Transformer to predict the complete expression, including its constants, in one step. The predicted constants can then serve as an informed starting point for optional numerical refinement. This changes the model's responsibility: it learns to propose both the form of the equation and the numbers needed to make that equation useful.

Ablation experiments support the end-to-end approach, with improvements sometimes appearing even without refinement. On problems from SRBench, the model approaches the performance of leading genetic-programming methods while providing inference several orders of magnitude faster. The stated result combines competitive equation recovery with much faster prediction, without claiming that the Transformer consistently surpasses genetic programming in accuracy.
neurips-2022-end-to-end-symbolic-regress.tldr: A Transformer predicts complete equations with constants, approaching leading genetic-programming performance with much faster inference.

paragraphs: Lightweight convolutional networks aim to make prediction fast enough for mobile applications. Their local convolution windows, however, limit how directly they capture relationships between distant image regions. Adding self-attention can supply global information, but its practical speed cost creates a problem for architectures designed around efficient inference.

GhostNetV2 introduces DFC attention, a mechanism built from fully connected layers that captures dependencies between distant pixels while executing efficiently on common hardware. The authors apply it to features expanded through GhostNet's inexpensive operations. A resulting block combines local information with longer-range relationships, addressing an expressiveness bottleneck in the earlier architecture.

Experiments report improvements over existing architectures. One concrete result is 75.3% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 167 million floating-point operations, compared with GhostNetV1's 74.5% at similar computational cost. This comparison supports the value of enriching cheaply generated features with broader context. The architecture's contribution is therefore both where it adds attention and how it implements that attention for mobile-oriented computation.
neurips-2022-ghostnetv2-enhance-cheap-op.tldr: GhostNetV2 enriches inexpensive convolutional features with hardware-friendly long-range attention, improving ImageNet accuracy at similar computational cost.

paragraphs: Retrosynthetic planning searches for a sequence of reactions that can produce a target molecule. Predicting feasible individual reactions is only part of that problem: the planner must also choose which sequence to pursue. The paper focuses on this decision-making policy, including whether the resulting routes meet a chemist's preferences for starting materials.

Existing strategies use either costly, high-variance online rollouts or a fixed value network trained on simulated routes with limited diversity and no negative feedback. GRASP introduces a goal-driven actor-critic framework to navigate the search toward a user-specified objective. This makes the desired outcome part of the policy's planning task.

Experiments on Pistachio and a dataset designed by chemists report improvements of up to 32.2% in search efficiency and 5.6% in quality over leading approaches. User studies also show successful planning toward designated building-block goals. These findings support goal-directed control of synthesis-route search, with the reported gains applying to the evaluated settings and the specified planning objectives.
neurips-2022-grasp-navigating-retrosynth.tldr: GRASP uses a goal-driven actor-critic policy to improve retrosynthetic search and produce routes aligned with requested building materials.

paragraphs: An image classifier can recognize a category by relying on associated visual cues instead of the object itself. This paper examines classes where that problem is especially severe. The authors select 15 ImageNet classes with strong spurious cues and collect object segmentation masks to create Hard ImageNet.

The masks support tests that distinguish the object from other image content. Using noise, saliency, and ablation measures, the authors find much stronger reliance on spurious features than in RIVAL10, an ImageNet counterpart to CIFAR10. Hard ImageNet objects also tend to occupy less image area and sit farther from the center, which the authors connect to greater reliance on surrounding cues.

The paper additionally uses robust neural features to rank images by the strength of their spurious cues. Comparing high- and low-ranked images within a class reveals specific cues used by models and poorer performance when those cues disappear. The dataset combines rankings, segmentations, and evaluation tools to make these dependencies easier to identify and study.
neurips-2022-hard-imagenet-segmentations.tldr: Hard ImageNet provides object masks and image rankings for 15 classes where classifiers strongly depend on spurious visual cues.

paragraphs: Stochastic neural networks produce predictions by averaging multiple realizations of a random function. An attacker estimating a gradient therefore uses one set of samples, while the eventual prediction uses another. This paper studies how that separation affects robustness against attacks constructed from sampled gradients.

The authors derive a sufficient condition for a stochastic prediction to withstand a given sample-based attack. Their analysis explains why drawing more samples to construct an adversarial example strengthens the attack, yet does not fully eliminate the effect of stochasticity. It also explains why the number of samples used during inference does not affect robustness in the analyzed account.

The theory connects greater robustness with higher gradient variance and a smaller magnitude of the expected gradient. These relationships organize several previously proposed ways of strengthening attacks or improving model robustness within one explanation. Extensive experiments verify the theoretical findings. The guarantee remains a sufficient condition against the given sample-based attack, preserving the distinction between this analysis and an unrestricted claim about all adversarial attacks.
neurips-2022-how-sampling-impacts-the-ro.tldr: A sufficient robustness condition explains how attack sampling and gradient statistics affect stochastic neural networks' resistance to sampled-gradient attacks.

paragraphs: Generating useful 3D shapes requires more than producing plausible point clouds. The paper also targets flexible manipulation and the ability to produce smooth surfaces or meshes. LION addresses these needs through a hierarchical variational autoencoder whose latent representation combines a global description of a shape with a representation organized as points.

Two hierarchical diffusion models learn to generate within these latent spaces. The authors report that this arrangement improves performance over diffusion directly on point clouds, while retaining a point-structured representation suited to diffusion modeling. The autoencoder framework also supports encoding existing shapes and interpolating between their latent representations.

LION achieves state-of-the-art generation performance on multiple ShapeNet benchmarks and performs strongly on multimodal shape denoising and voxel-conditioned synthesis. The authors also describe adaptation to text- and image-driven generation. Adding surface reconstruction techniques produces smooth meshes. Together, these capabilities connect shape generation with editing, conditioning, and surface output, addressing several distinct requirements of tools intended for artists working with 3D content.
neurips-2022-lion-latent-point-diffusion.tldr: LION generates 3D shapes through hierarchical latent diffusion and supports conditioning, interpolation, denoising, and smooth mesh reconstruction.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to capture separate factors of variation in separate aspects of a model's internal representation. Yet models with highly disentangled representations can fail on unfamiliar combinations of familiar factor values. This paper investigates why that happens, addressing a tension with earlier findings of improved performance outside the training distribution.

The central question separates two possible failures: an encoder might place an unfamiliar combination in the wrong latent region, or a decoder might fail to render it despite receiving a correct representation. Across several models, datasets, and training settings, the authors find that failed generalization is accompanied by incorrect encoder placement of unseen combinations.

Observed successes also require careful interpretation. In the tested settings, they occur either when too few examples have been excluded or when exclusions combine object properties with shape. The authors argue that capturing distinct factors is insufficient by itself: models also need to understand how to invert the process producing the visual input. This frames successful encoding as a central part of compositional generalization.
neurips-2022-lost-in-latent-space-examin.tldr: Experiments link failures on unseen factor combinations to incorrect latent encoding and qualify when disentangled models appear to generalize successfully.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning estimates the reward and associated optimal policy that best explain an expert's observed behavior. Many methods repeatedly solve a policy problem inside a separate reward-estimation loop. That nested structure is expensive in high-dimensional environments, while shortcuts emphasizing policy estimation can sacrifice reward accuracy.

The paper proposes a single-loop method that follows each policy-improvement step with a stochastic gradient update for likelihood maximization. It is designed to reduce the nested computation without compromising reward estimation. Accurate rewards matter because they support counterfactual questions, such as how an optimal policy should change when the environment's dynamics change or when addressing new tasks.

The authors prove finite-time convergence to a stationary solution. Under linear reward parameterization, they further show that the identified solution corresponds to the maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning solution. Experiments on MuJoCo robotics control problems and transfer settings report superior performance against evaluated inverse reinforcement learning and imitation-learning methods. The theoretical result thus pairs a general stationarity guarantee with a stronger identification result under a specific reward assumption.
neurips-2022-maximum-likelihood-inverse-.tldr: A single-loop inverse reinforcement learning algorithm preserves reward estimation and provides finite-time convergence to a stationary solution.

paragraphs: Cloud prediction services expose two related confidentiality concerns. Model extraction attempts to reproduce a deployed model's behavior, while membership inference tries to determine whether particular data belonged to its training set. This paper shows that the two attacks can reinforce one another through an iterative process, improving extraction and reducing membership-inference query costs.

The proposed MExMI framework incorporates membership inference into pool-based active model extraction. Its three components are an MI pre-filter, an MI post-filter, and semi-supervised boosting. The overall approach uses the connection between the attacks to improve the extraction process while also making membership inference more economical in its use of prediction queries.

Experiments report extraction improvement of up to 11.14% over the best-known pool-based active extraction attack and 94.07% fidelity with 16,000 queries. Membership-inference precision and recall are comparable to a state-of-the-art attack requiring 150,000 queries. These findings demonstrate that evaluating the two threats together can reveal a more effective attack process than treating their capabilities separately.
neurips-2022-mexmi-pool-based-active-mod.tldr: MExMI combines model extraction and membership inference so that each attack improves the other's effectiveness or query efficiency.

paragraphs: Data-free knowledge distillation trains a student to learn from a teacher without using the original training data. A generator supplies synthetic examples instead. As that generator changes, its examples come from a changing distribution; adversarial training can make the changes large enough that the student forgets knowledge acquired earlier.

Momentum Adversarial Distillation maintains an exponential moving average copy of the generator. The student trains on examples from both the current generator and this averaged copy. Because the averaged generator incorporates earlier versions and often changes more gradually, its samples can help preserve earlier knowledge while moderating the student's adaptation to the newest examples.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and Places365, show better performance than competing methods for handling large distribution shifts. The method also compares favorably with existing data-free distillation approaches and reaches state-of-the-art results in some cases. Its central contribution is a way to stabilize the synthetic training distribution while retaining samples from the actively updated generator.
neurips-2022-momentum-adversarial-distil.tldr: Training on samples from both current and averaged generators helps data-free distillation reduce forgetting during large synthetic-data shifts.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification predicts a set of labels for each input. Carefully chosen, visually imperceptible changes can manipulate that set. The paper argues that adapting existing provable defenses from multiclass classification produces suboptimal guarantees for this setting and introduces MultiGuard to address the multi-label problem directly.

MultiGuard wraps an arbitrary multi-label classifier with randomized smoothing, using isotropic Gaussian noise on the input. Its main theorem guarantees that a certain number of an input's true labels remain in the predicted set when the adversarial perturbation has bounded Euclidean, or l2, norm. This expresses protection in terms of retained correct labels.

The authors also provide an algorithm for computing the robustness guarantees and evaluate the method on VOC 2007, MS-COCO, and NUS-WIDE. The guarantee is specifically about how many true labels remain present within the permitted perturbation size; it does not assert that every predicted label is unchanged. That formulation makes the certificate directly relevant to predictions that can contain multiple simultaneous labels.
neurips-2022-multiguard-provably-robust-.tldr: MultiGuard certifies that a certain number of true labels survive adversarial perturbations with bounded l2 norm.

paragraphs: This paper studies random embeddings for signals with rank-one Kronecker structure. Such signals have a tensor organization built from component factors, and the analysis explicitly uses that structure. The question concerns near-isometric behavior: how a random embedding can preserve the geometric size of signals in the class being considered.

The main result is a uniform concentration inequality for random tensors acting on these structured signals. Uniformity makes the result concern the signal class collectively, rather than only a single selected signal. The authors describe the inequality as a counterpart to a Gordon-type inequality for this tensor-structured setting, connecting the analysis to an established kind of geometric probability bound.

The paper considers two variants of the random embedding. Their embedding dimensions depend on explicit quantities describing signal complexity, making that complexity central to the dimension requirements. Examples from signal recovery and optimization illustrate applications of the developed tools. The contribution is therefore a theoretical framework for structured embeddings, accompanied by examples showing where its guarantees can be used.
neurips-2022-near-isometric-properties-o.tldr: Uniform concentration bounds connect random tensor embedding dimensions to the complexity of rank-one Kronecker-structured signals.

paragraphs: Tensor completion reconstructs missing entries in a multidimensional array from observed entries. The paper addresses the special case where entries are nonnegative. Its starting point is a gap with matrix completion: for general tensor completion, no algorithm is known to achieve the information-theoretic sample complexity rate.

The authors introduce a norm for nonnegative tensors using the gauge of a particular polytope defined by zero-one structure. Integer linear programming solves the associated linear separation problems. Combining that geometric construction with a variant of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm yields a numerical method that connects the statistical completion objective to discrete optimization.

The paper proves that the method achieves the information-theoretic rate and gives an oracle-step convergence guarantee described as linear in numerical tolerance. Computational experiments demonstrate effectiveness and scalability on tensors containing up to one hundred million entries using a laptop. The result joins a sample-efficiency guarantee with practical demonstrations, while the algorithm and theorem specifically target the nonnegative case.
neurips-2022-nonnegative-tensor-completi.tldr: A nonnegative tensor-completion algorithm combines integer optimization with Frank-Wolfe updates and achieves the information-theoretic sample complexity rate.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds seek to control the difference between a learning algorithm's training performance and its performance beyond the training data. This paper derives information-theoretic bounds using a new quantity called leave-one-out conditional mutual information, or loo-CMI. The motivation is practical as well as theoretical: other CMI-based bounds can be difficult to evaluate.

The proposed bounds are easier to compute and admit connections to several familiar ways of understanding learning. These include leave-one-out cross-validation, optimization stability, and the geometry of the loss landscape. The framework applies both to the output of a training algorithm and to its predictions, providing two places at which the information-based analysis can be used.

The authors evaluate the predicted generalization gap in deep-learning settings and obtain non-vacuous bounds on image-classification tasks. Non-vacuous means the guarantee provides meaningful information rather than an uninformative allowance for error. The findings support loo-CMI as a usable approach to generalization analysis, combining interpretable connections with empirical evidence that the bounds can be informative.
neurips-2022-on-leave-one-out-conditiona.tldr: Leave-one-out conditional mutual information yields easier-to-compute generalization bounds that are non-vacuous on evaluated image-classification tasks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much a neural network's available function class can be constrained in advance while retaining training error comparable to an unconstrained model. It calls the removable portion excess capacity and measures capacity through empirical Rademacher complexity. The question concerns supervised classification and includes modern architectures such as residual networks.

To support that investigation, the authors extend and unify complexity bounds to handle composed functions, added functions, and convolutional structure. The main capacity-related quantities are layer Lipschitz constants and a group-norm measure of how far convolutional weights move from initialization. These quantities provide a way to constrain capacity through properties of the weights.

Experiments across benchmark tasks of different difficulty indicate substantial excess capacity for each task. They also suggest that capacity can be held at surprisingly similar levels across tasks while retaining comparable empirical error. The authors interpret this as a form of compressibility through weight norms, complementary to pruning. The findings concern the studied capacity measure and empirical performance, making the choice of measurement central to their interpretation.
neurips-2022-on-measuring-excess-capacit.tldr: Complexity bounds and experiments suggest networks can retain comparable training error under substantial constraints on weight-based capacity.

paragraphs: Modern networks often repeat similar modules many times, increasing representational capacity but also storage requirements. Parameter-Efficient Masking Networks investigate how much can be represented using fixed random weights with only a limited number of unique values. Learning focuses on diverse masks that allow those shared values to support different feature mappings.

For architectures with repetitive structure, the method uses one randomly initialized layer together with different learned masks to represent multiple modules. The stored model can therefore be expressed through that layer and its masks, substantially reducing storage cost. Different mappings arise from the masks applied to the shared random weights.

The authors extend the strategy by filling a model through padding from a given random weight vector and then learning masks. This further lowers space complexity, particularly for architectures with less repetition. Experiments across different network architectures evaluate both the representational potential of the masks and their usefulness for compression. The contribution centers on storing and reusing limited random values while learning how each module uses them.
neurips-2022-parameter-efficient-masking.tldr: Parameter-Efficient Masking Networks reduce model storage by learning different masks over shared, fixed random weights with limited unique values.

paragraphs: Standard nonconvex optimization analyses often assume that gradients cannot change too rapidly, formalized through Lipschitz smoothness. Some deep-learning objectives instead satisfy a weaker condition that allows unbounded smoothness. Gradient clipping has established advantages over ordinary stochastic gradient descent in that setting, motivating the question of whether explicit clipping is essential.

The paper analyzes a generalized SignSGD family ranging from SignSGD to an algorithm closely resembling Adam. Under the relaxed smoothness assumption, it proves convergence rates similar to clipped SGD without requiring an explicit clipping operation. Momentum plays a central role: it reduces noise and also weakens the impact of unbounded smoothness and gradient magnitudes.

The noise reduction removes the need for large minibatches imposed by earlier SignSGD analyses. The authors also identify a theoretical benefit of Adam-type methods over nonadaptive methods in this setting. Experiments on deep-learning tasks match Adam's performance while outperforming the other compared optimizers. These findings support a specific explanation for adaptive optimization's behavior under the paper's relaxed smoothness model.
neurips-2022-robustness-to-unbounded-smo.tldr: Generalized SignSGD uses momentum to attain clipped-SGD-like convergence rates under relaxed smoothness assumptions without explicit gradient clipping.

paragraphs: Error-correcting output codes support multiclass classification through a codebook whose rows represent classes and whose columns organize binary classification decisions. Designing a codebook with strong error correction becomes difficult as the number of classes or columns grows. This paper addresses that design problem with a mixed-integer quadratically constrained optimization formulation.

The formulation accommodates multiple design criteria while targeting error-correction capability. A tractable procedure grows the codebook by adding columns chosen for their gains in that capability. The authors show that a graph-coloring problem provides an upper bound on the maximal gain, enabling efficient generation of near-optimal codebooks for large instances.

The resulting classifiers are competitive on MNIST and CIFAR10. With transfer-learned binary classifiers, they outperform transfer-learned multiclass convolutional networks on CIFAR100 and Caltech-101/256. These results support the practical value of a modular classification system built around optimized codes. The contribution combines a scalable construction procedure with a way to assess how close its error-correction gains are to an upper bound.
neurips-2022-scalable-design-of-error-co.tldr: Discrete optimization and graph-coloring bounds enable scalable, near-optimal error-correcting codebooks with competitive multiclass classification performance.

paragraphs: A model can perform well overall while serving particular subgroups poorly. This paper examines that concern in tabular data, where sensitive groups can be clearly defined and fairness problems arise in real applications. The authors focus on an evaluation gap: studies of fairness and robustness methods often omit strong tree-based models from their comparisons.

They compare existing fair and robust learning methods with tree-based methods and other baselines across eight datasets and more than 340,000 model configurations. Tree-based approaches show strong subgroup robustness, including against methods explicitly designed to improve fairness or robustness. The best tree models also tend to perform well across multiple evaluation measures.

Some robust or group-fair models, by comparison, vary substantially across metrics even when the model itself is fixed. Tree-based models are also less sensitive to hyperparameter settings and less expensive to train in the study. These empirical findings support tree ensembles as an effective baseline and a sensible default for tabular subgroup robustness, without establishing that they win on every dataset or criterion.
neurips-2022-subgroup-robustness-grows-o.tldr: A large tabular-data comparison finds tree ensembles strong, economical baselines for subgroup robustness across multiple metrics.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are used in applications where computational efficiency matters, but they can also be vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Certified training approaches developed for conventional artificial neural networks cannot be transferred directly because spiking networks use different neuron behavior and input formats. This paper develops tools that account for those differences.

The authors introduce S-IBP and S-CROWN to handle nonlinear functions in spiking-neuron models. They also formalize bounds for both digital inputs and spike inputs. Together, these components provide the basis for a robust training method tailored to spiking networks, addressing both the neurons' computations and the forms in which inputs arrive.

Experiments across different datasets and model architectures demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The abstract reports a maximum attack-error reduction of 37.7% with a 3.7% loss in original accuracy. This presents an empirical robustness–accuracy tradeoff in the evaluated settings. The main contribution is adapting the machinery needed for certified training to spiking behavior, rather than assuming conventional-network certifications apply unchanged.
neurips-2022-toward-robust-spiking-neura.tldr: S-IBP and S-CROWN enable robust training tailored to spiking neurons and inputs, with reported attack-error reductions at an accuracy cost.

paragraphs: VideoMAE studies whether video transformers can learn useful representations without extra large-scale pretraining datasets. It uses self-supervised reconstruction: the model learns from videos by recovering hidden content. The proposed tube-masking design removes an unusually high fraction of the video, making reconstruction a demanding task that encourages useful representation learning.

Masking 90% to 95% of the input still produces favorable performance. The authors explain that video's temporal redundancy permits more aggressive masking than images. They also obtain strong results with roughly 3,000 to 4,000 videos and no extra data, attributing part of that effectiveness to reconstruction requiring the model to learn high-level structure.

The experiments additionally emphasize data quality and the mismatch between pretraining and target domains. Using a standard vision-transformer backbone, VideoMAE reports results across four video benchmarks without extra data. Taken together, the findings support highly masked reconstruction as a data-efficient pretraining strategy and show why the suitability of the training videos matters alongside their number.
neurips-2022-videomae-masked-autoencoder.tldr: VideoMAE learns useful video representations by reconstructing inputs with 90–95% masking, achieving strong results even with small datasets.

paragraphs: Autoregressive dance generators predict motion sequentially, and accumulated noise can eventually make their movement freeze. The paper addresses this failure with two modules that can be added to existing models. Both use a bank of latent codes to improve how predicted motion is represented and how future motion is anticipated.

The first module learns a low-dimensional motion representation through an autoencoder with the code bank. Because high-dimensional motion predictions can be overwhelmed by noise, this learned representation provides a way to reduce that noise and prevent freezing. The second module extends the bank to supply explicit prior information about future movements, helping resolve ambiguity in prediction.

That future information helps predictors produce larger movements with higher fidelity. Experiments on the AIST++ 3D dance benchmark report improvements over baselines in quality, diversity, and sequence length. The results connect two aspects of sustained dance generation: keeping predictions from deteriorating through accumulated noise and giving the predictor stronger guidance about what movement can come next.
neurips-2022-you-never-stop-dancing-non-.tldr: A latent-code bank reduces motion noise and supplies future-motion guidance, helping dance generators produce longer, more diverse sequences without freezing.
